title: Install Python in Termux: Build and Run Your First Python App with Nano on Android
voiceover: I tried running my first Python automation script inside Termux while waiting for a train and watched the screen freeze on a wall of compiler errors. Nothing was broken on my phone; I had simply missed the two build flags and Android-specific package requirements that mobile Linux demands behind the scenes. Once you understand how Python lives inside Termux's sandbox, writing, editing with nano, and executing production-ready scripts on your phone takes less than ten minutes.

title: Step 1: Installing Python and Core Dependencies in Termux
voiceover: Before installing any language runtime, always synchronise your package database with the official mirrors. Termux updates packages frequently, and attempting to install packages against a stale cache is the number one cause of broken package downloads: Once the system packages are up to date, install Python.

title: Step 2: Exploring the Python Interactive Shell (REPL)
voiceover: The quickest way to confirm that your Python environment can execute code is by launching the interactive Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL). Type python into your terminal and hit Enter: The terminal cursor will transform into the classic triple-arrow prompt ( >>> ).

title: Step 3: Configuring Nano for Painless Python Indentation
voiceover: Interactive shells are great for one-liners, but real applications need script files. On a desktop computer, developers use IDEs with automatic indentation and linting.

title: Step 4: Building the Demo App: Pocket Task and System Monitor
voiceover: Now let's build a real, useful demo application rather than a trivial one-line hello world. We will create Pocket Tracker ( pocket_tracker.py ): an interactive command-line application that allows you to manage tasks with persistent JSON storage on your phone and inspect real-time system metrics (timestamp, battery-friendly memory usage, and free disk storage).

title: Step 5: Running and Testing Your Python App in Termux
voiceover: With your code saved to disk, you can execute it in two different ways. The direct approach is passing the filename as an argument to the Python interpreter: Alternatively, you can give your script direct executable permissions with chmod , allowing you to run it like any native command via the shebang line ( #!/usr/bin/env python3 ) at the top of the file: Try interacting with your new application: Now check your project folder with ls -la .

voiceover: Python's built-in standard library is powerful, but modern development relies heavily on third-party packages from PyPI (Python Package Index). bullets: Update your package index with pkg update && pkg upgrade and install the runtime with pkg install python .
Configure ~/.nanorc with set tabstospaces and set tabsize 4 to prevent mixed-indentation syntax crashes.
Create your script using nano filename.py , write your logic, save with Ctrl+O , and exit with Ctrl+X .
Execute your app with python filename.py or grant execute permissions with chmod +x filename.py .
